previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A patient with Type 1 diabetes and a history of gastroparesis was admitted for an acute episode of nausea and vomiting. She was treated with IV anti-emetics and fluids, and her diet was gradually advanced as symptoms improved. Initial concerns about an abnormal chest X-ray and elevated cardiac enzymes were resolved with repeat imaging and labs, showing no evidence of pneumonia or myocardial injury. Her blood glucose was well-controlled during the hospitalization. New medications, including aspirin and lisinopril, were started for long-term protection against diabetic complications. The gastric pacemaker appeared intact, with outpatient interrogation planned. She was discharged home in stable condition, tolerating oral intake, with follow-up arranged.

Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted to the hospital for a gastroparesis flare. As 
you are aware gastroparesis occurs as a complication of your 
diabetes. Controlling your blood sugars helps to prevent 
gastroparesis flares and reduce nausea. You should NOT eat large 
meals, self-induce vomiting, or drink large quantities of soda 
as these behaviors will prescipitate a gastroparesis flare and 
make you feel ill. You should NEVER skip taking insulin, even if 
you CANNOT EAT, as you can make yourself ill.

If you do have nausea, please take compazine as prescribed.  I 
have also included a rectal fomula for compazine, and if you 
cannot tolerate pills, you need to take rectal compazine for 
nausea.

Please keep you follow-up appointments with your primary care 
provider and the ___ Clinic. Please take all your medications 
as prescribed.

You are to start a baby aspirin to protect your heart from a 
heart attack. You are to start taking lisinopril to protect your 
kidney from diabetes damage. You are being given  anti-nausea 
medication that you can take as needed.

If you develop worsening nausea or vomiting, fever, chest pain, 
difficulty breathing, abdominal pain or any other concerning 
medical symptom, please call your doctor or 911.
